e.etymology: From an English surname meaning son of Eddie, a pet form of Edward. As a first name it honors the inventor Thomas Edison.
namesakes: Thomas Edison (inventor of the phonograph and the practical light bulb)

assoc.t: Edison bulbs, vintage-style filament light bulbs

e.etymology: From Spanish rey, king, used as a given name and as a short form of Reynaldo and Reyes. Girls' use rose after Rey, the heroine of the Star Wars sequels, appeared in 2015.

assoc.t: heroine of the Star Wars sequel trilogy

e.etymology: For girls, a spelling of Valerie, from French Valérie and the Roman family name Valeria, from Latin valere, to be strong. Valery is also a Russian and French men's name from Valerius.
Mainly a short form of Raymond, from Germanic ragin, counsel, and mund, protection. It also comes from surnames with several sources, among them Old French rei, king.
namesakes: Ray Romano (star of Everybody Loves Raymond)
Ray Lewis (Hall of Fame NFL linebacker)

assoc.t: ray, a beam of light or sunshine
Ray Charles, soul and R&B pioneer

e.etymology: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Alfred, from Old English Aelfraed: aelf, elf, and raed, counsel.

assoc.t: Alfredo sauce, the creamy pasta sauce of fettuccine Alfredo

e.note: In the US the bare name calls up Alfredo pasta sauce.

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Shea, from the Irish surname O Seaghdha, usually explained as hawk-like or admirable. In Ireland it is also a short form of Seamus, and it can render Hebrew Shai, gift.
From an English surname going back to the Old English woman's name Cyneburg, royal fortress, or to a Devon place name. As a modern first name it also serves as a short form of Kimberly.

assoc.t: American firearms maker known for 1911 pistols

e.etymology: An American combination of Nova, Latin for new, and Lee. It is the name of the heroine Novalee Nation in the novel and film Where the Heart Is.
namesakes: Novalee Nation (Natalie Portman's character in Where the Heart Is)

assoc.t: Novalee Nation, heroine of Where the Heart Is

e.etymology: A K spelling of Cannon, an English and Irish surname that is also the word for the big gun. Kannon is separately the Japanese name of the Buddhist bodhisattva of mercy.

assoc.t: sounds like cannon, the large gun
Japanese name of the Buddhist bodhisattva of mercy

e.etymology: The medieval English spoken form of Henry, from Old French Henri and Germanic Heimirich, home ruler. Later it also became a pet form of Harold.
namesakes: Harry Potter (boy wizard of J.K. Rowling's novels)

assoc.t: Harry's, men's razor and grooming brand

e.note: In most American accents it sounds the same as the word hairy.

e.etymology: From Old French Rogier, from a Frankish name built from hrod, fame, and ger, spear. The Normans brought it to England.
namesakes: Roger Rabbit (cartoon star of Who Framed Roger Rabbit)

assoc.t: roger that, radio talk for message received

e.note: Roger is radio shorthand for understood; in British slang, to roger is a crude word for sex.

e.etymology: A feminine form of George with -ina, from Greek georgos, farmer or earth-worker. Its recent US rise follows Georgina Rodriguez of the Netflix series I Am Georgina.
namesakes: Georgina Rodriguez (model, Cristiano Ronaldo's partner and star of I Am Georgina)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage in the family of Janiyah and Saniyah, built on the popular -iyah ending.
A late 20th-century American coinage joining the Brae- or Bray- sound with the -lyn ending; compare Braylen and Braylon.
From Hebrew Chanokh, dedicated, by way of Greek and Latin. In Genesis, Enoch walked with God and was the father of Methuselah.
namesakes: Enoch (Genesis patriarch who walked with God)
Nucky Thompson (Boardwalk Empire boss, born Enoch)

e.etymology: A Spanish name taken from the surname of Saint Philip Benizi, a 13th-century Italian priest known in Spanish as San Felipe Benicio.
namesakes: Benicio del Toro (Oscar-winning actor in Traffic and Sicario)

e.etymology: From Spanish solana, a sunny spot or the sunny side of a hill, from sol, sun; also a Spanish surname and place name.
A modern respelling of Landon, an English surname from a place name, a variant of Langdon, long hill.
From an English surname meaning son of Jeffrey. In the US it is given in honor of Thomas Jefferson, the third president.
namesakes: Thomas Jefferson (third US president, author of the Declaration of Independence)

e.etymology: A short form of Anthony, from the Roman family name Antonius, whose origin is unknown. It has been given as a full name since the 19th century.
namesakes: Tony Soprano (mob boss of The Sopranos)

assoc.t: Tony the Tiger, Frosted Flakes mascot

e.etymology: From Latin magnus, great. An eleventh-century king of Norway took it from Charlemagne's title Carolus Magnus, and it spread through Scandinavia and to Scotland.
namesakes: Magnus Bane (warlock in the Shadowhunters books and series)

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Bryson, an English surname meaning son of Brice. It can also be read as Bryce with the popular -en ending.
A spelling of Savannah, used in the US since the 1800s after the Georgia city and river. It matches the word savanna, a grassy plain, which came through Spanish from the Taino language.

assoc.t: savanna, a grassy plain with scattered trees

e.etymology: The Latin and Greek Bible form of Noah, from Hebrew Noach, rest. As Noé it is the everyday Spanish and French form of the name.
From an English surname, Ellis plus -son; Ellis is the medieval English form of Elias, the Greek form of Elijah.
Shortened from María de Araceli, a Spanish title of the Virgin Mary as patron of Lucena in Andalusia, from Latin ara coeli, altar of heaven.
A short form of Tyler, Tyrone, Tyson and other names beginning with Ty, used as a full name since the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Ty Pennington (Extreme Makeover: Home Edition host)

assoc.t: maker of Beanie Babies plush toys

e.etymology: From an English and Scottish surname, a variant of Brook or a nickname for someone thought to resemble a badger, brock in Middle English.

assoc.t: Brock, Ash's friend and gym leader in Pokemon

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Biblical Mishael, Hebrew for who is what God is. Mishael was one of Daniel's three companions, renamed Meshach in Babylon.
Two names share this spelling. Arabic Idris is a prophet in the Quran, often identified with Enoch; Welsh Idris joins udd, lord, and ris, ardent, and names the giant of the mountain Cadair Idris.
namesakes: Idris Elba (actor in Luther and The Wire)

e.etymology: A variant spelling of Isaac, from Hebrew Yitzchak, he will laugh; in Genesis, the son of Abraham and Sarah.
e.note: Often taken for a misspelling of Isaac.

e.etymology: From Latin Evander, from Greek Euandros, good man. In Roman legend Evander founded a settlement on the future site of Rome.
